biggest_risk: Because the bulk of your savings sits inside the registered account, the forced minimum withdrawals once it converts to a Registered Retirement Income Fund could push your taxable income upward in your later years, just as the management fee quietly drains a meaningful slice of growth every year.
best_lever: The single move that would shift your odds the most is lowering the management fee on your portfolio, since that cost compounds against you across every remaining year of accumulation and retirement.
snapshot_intro: Your plan earns a solid grade and holds up in the clear majority of tested paths, which is a reassuring place to stand a few years out from retirement. This result reflects thousands of tested scenarios — including severe crashes and prolonged inflation — but cannot capture every possible risk such as legislative changes, major health issues, or divorce. Treat this assessment as a starting point; the first step of looking clearly at the numbers is the one that matters most.
mirror_block: You are a few short years from the retirement age you have chosen, with your partner planning to step away around the same time. Between you, you have built a substantial nest egg, most of it inside a registered account, alongside a tax-free account, a smaller non-registered slice, and a home that will be nearly clear of its mortgage by then. In retirement your income would lean on government benefits and an employer pension as a steady floor, with your portfolio topping up the rest. The piece to watch is how heavily your wealth leans on that one registered account and the fee it carries year after year.
revenue_analysis: The income you would replace in retirement covers a good part of what you earn today, which suggests your lifestyle could carry forward without a jarring drop. The structure helps here: a guaranteed floor from pensions and government benefits would handle the bulk of routine spending, leaving the portfolio to cover the remainder rather than the whole. That layering is what would let your day-to-day feel steady even when markets wobble.
savings_analysis: Your savings are on a clear upward path between now and retirement, driven less by new contributions than by the years of compounding still ahead on the balance you have already built. The runway the plan shows would carry well beyond a typical retirement length, which is the core source of your confidence. The takeaway is that the foundation is set — what remains is shaping how efficiently that capital is held and drawn.
gov_explanation: The guaranteed-income floor is the calm bedrock of this plan — it arrives for life and would cover most of your household spending target once both of you have begun collecting. Before that, in the bridge years after you stop working but before government benefits start, your employer pension is already flowing as a guaranteed base, with your savings covering the remainder of spending rather than the whole. Recognizing those two phases as distinct matters, because your portfolio leans on hardest early — alongside that pension — and then eases as the full lifetime floor switches on.
cpp_timing: Claiming Canada Pension Plan earlier shows a slightly stronger success rate in your scenarios than claiming at the standard age, while waiting until the latest age pulls it lower — largely because deferring leans harder on your portfolio through the bridge years. You can toggle between the claiming ages with the pills to see how each reshapes the path. The right choice depends on factors beyond the model, so treat these as views rather than a verdict.
longevity_analysis: Half of the scenarios we ran land your capital somewhere between a cautious lower figure and a far more favorable upper one — a wide band that reflects how much markets can swing over a long retirement. Even the cautious end of that range keeps your plan intact, which is the reassuring part. You can hover over the fan chart to see how this range narrows or widens at any age along the way.
spending_flex: Your plan carries built-in spending flexibility, with the ability to trim a meaningful share of withdrawals in lean years. Notably, the simulations never actually triggered those cuts, meaning the flexibility sat in reserve as a safety valve rather than a tool you would routinely need. The spending smile chart lets you hover to see how your estimated spending naturally eases through the later phases.
what_if_analysis: The scenario that moves your success rate most is lowering the management fee, which lifts the plan well above where it sits today and adds a noticeably higher projected median. That single change outweighs saving more, which barely shifts the result — a clear signal that for you the cost of holding investments matters more than adding to them.
strategy_comparison: Among the paths tested, the low MER approach stands apart: it raises your success rate well above the status-quo plan and lifts the projected median capital with it. By contrast, saving more leaves the result essentially unchanged, and delaying Canada Pension Plan to the latest age actually pulls the success rate down — which tells you the leverage here is in what you keep, not what you add.
sequence_risk: The spread between the cautious and favorable ends of your portfolio range comes largely from timing: two identical portfolios can end up worlds apart depending on whether the rough markets hit early or late. Poor returns in your first retirement years bite hardest, because there is less time to recover — though your employer pension already carries part of the bridge, so the portfolio only has to cover the remainder of spending during that stretch. That cushion would soften, without erasing, how much early markets matter.
priority_actions: The reason fees matter so much for you specifically is time and concentration: with a sizeable balance compounding over a long retirement, a management fee near the upper end of retail quietly skims a meaningful slice every single year, and that slice grows as the balance does. Translated into lifestyle terms, the difference could amount to many months of retirement income over the life of the plan — money that simply never reaches you. What is already protected is the structure itself: your guaranteed pensions and benefits form a floor that no fee or market dip can erase, so this lever is about keeping more of the surplus, not rescuing the foundation.
tax_analysis: Your effective tax rate today and in retirement sit close together, so you are not facing a dramatic cliff when work income stops. The slim year-to-year difference suggests the bigger tax story is not your rate but the timing of withdrawals from a registered-heavy portfolio. That gives you room to think about sequencing well before mandatory withdrawals begin.
fees_analysis: At a management fee near the upper end of retail pricing, the lifetime cost works out to a sum equal to many months of retirement income lost over the plan's span. Because that cost compounds on a growing balance, it is the quiet drag that the what-if scenarios flag as your single biggest lever. The interactive fee chart lets you hover across several fee levels to see how steeply that line diverges over time.
couple_analysis: As a couple retiring around the same time, the order in which you draw from each account and how you share pension income would shape your combined tax bracket more than any single account does alone. If the primary earner were to pass first, the surviving partner would keep their own pensions plus a survivor Canada Pension Plan benefit, and the tax-free account would transfer tax-free — though total household income would step down. If the partner were to pass first, the primary would retain all the registered accounts, with the partner's own savings folding in. Either way, the guaranteed pensions soften the transition rather than leaving a cliff.
property_analysis: Your home represents a large share of your overall wealth, yet the projection never sells it or draws on its equity. That leaves it as a frozen standby reserve — valuable, but not part of your monthly income unless you choose to unlock it later. Its main role here is reassurance: a substantial asset sitting behind the plan should circumstances ever call for it.
strengths_risks: Your strengths are clear: a guaranteed-income floor that would cover most of your monthly target for life, a near-paid-off home worth a substantial sum, and a combined nest egg with real depth. The risks are equally specific: the heavy concentration of registered savings in one account, a management fee whose lifetime cost runs into many months of income, and a short bridge where your savings cover the share of spending your employer pension does not yet reach before government benefits begin. None of these is a threat to survival — they are the dials worth watching as you fine-tune.
estate_analysis: In the median path, your estate would pass on a substantial sum, and even in the cautious case it remains a real legacy rather than nothing. That fits your balanced preference — neither spending everything down nor hoarding it untouched. The wide gap between those two figures is mostly a function of how markets and withdrawals interact over time, not a flaw in the plan.
obs_1: **Bridge funding** : The short stretch between stepping away from work and the start of government benefits would be carried partly by your employer pension, which already flows from the day you retire, with your savings covering the remainder rather than the whole. Because that savings draw comes early in retirement, it lands during the most sensitive window for your portfolio, which makes the cash set aside for it worth treating differently from your long-term holdings.
obs_2: **Income balance** : Your two incomes are uneven, which means the household leans somewhat more on one earner's flow today. That tilt would matter most for how you split income and pensions later to keep the combined tax bill in check, and it shapes how a survivor's finances would shift.
obs_3: **Home equity** : Your property holds significant value with only a small mortgage left, but that wealth sits frozen — it cannot be drawn on monthly without selling or borrowing. The plan deliberately leaves it untouched, so it functions as a standby reserve rather than part of your income engine.
obs_4: **Guaranteed floor** : Once both of you reach the steady-state age, your combined guaranteed income would draw from several streams — Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security, an employer pension that is not a government benefit, and your spouse's own benefits — together covering most of your monthly household target. The bridge years before this carry little government income, though your employer pension is already flowing then as a partial floor, with savings topping up the rest until the full steady-state coverage switches on.
obs_5: **Closing window** : With your retirement now near, your accumulation phase is in its final stretch, and the contributions you make from here compound for the shortest time. That does not diminish them, but it does mean the structural choices — fees, account mix, withdrawal order — carry more weight than raw saving at this point.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years just before you retire, while you are still earning, could be the most impactful window for shaping your fee structure and the order you would eventually draw accounts. These are decisions easiest to set before withdrawals begin rather than after. The next update of this assessment, in a year's time, would measure how any adjustments are tracking.
model_blind_spots: A few things this model does not capture could matter a great deal for you: how you split pension income between partners to manage the household bracket, the possibility of selling the home and unlocking its frozen value, and life events like an inheritance or a health change that reshape the picture. The uneven incomes between you also leave room for survivor-income shifts the base projection treats lightly. These dimensions could be explored in a future review.
